title: Homotopy invariance of each fixed-type hammock graph
statement:
Use small simplicial categories and weak homotopy equivalences of simplicial sets as in [lem-coef-coherent-nerve-comparison]. Use the ordinary fixed-word diagram categories and their nerves from [def-coef-zigzag-homotopy-calculus]. A wide simplicial subcategory has the same objects, simplicial subsets of the mapping sets, and contains identities and composites. Let $O$ be a small set, let $A,B$ be simplicial categories with object set $O$, let $U\subseteq A$, $V\subseteq B$ be wide simplicial subcategories, and let $S:A\to B$ fix objects and send $U$ into $V$. Assume that for every $a,b\in O$ both $A(a,b)\to B(a,b)$ and $U(a,b)\to V(a,b)$ are weak homotopy equivalences. Fix $x,y\in O$ and a finite word $w=(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_l)$ with letters $+$ and $-$. Define the bisimplicial set $D^w_{A,U}(x,y)_{p,q}$ to consist of commutative rectangular diagrams in the ordinary category $A_p$ with $q+1$ rows, $l$ horizontal columns, and endpoints $x,y$ in every row. All vertical arrows point down and belong to $U_p$, and the endpoint vertical arrows are identities. Column $i$ points right if $\epsilon_i=+$, and left with its arrows in $U_p$ if $\epsilon_i=-$. Identity columns and adjacent columns of the same direction are allowed; no reduction is imposed. In the $p$ direction apply the simplicial operators of $A,U$; in the $q$ direction delete or repeat rows, composing the intervening vertical arrows when a row is deleted. The length-zero diagram exists exactly when $x=y$. Define $D^w_{B,V}$ in the same way. Applying $S$ to every arrow gives a weak homotopy equivalence
$$\operatorname{diag}D^w_{A,U}(x,y)\longrightarrow\operatorname{diag}D^w_{B,V}(x,y)$$
for every $w,x,y$.

source.place: Dwyer–Kan, Calculating simplicial localizations, Definition 5.1 and Lemma 5.7, printed p.24; its proof uses Example 10.3 and Propositions 10.4–10.5. No Stacks tag states this result.

proof.text: First record the product consequence of [lem-coef-bisimplicial-diagonal-equivalence]. If $f:X\to X'$ is a weak homotopy equivalence and $K$ is any simplicial set, form the bisimplicial sets $X_p\times K_q$ and $X'_p\times K_q$. For fixed $q$, their map in the $p$ direction is a disjoint union of copies of $f$. Realization of this disjoint union is the disjoint union of realizations: each simplex stays in its indexed summand, so path components and all based homotopy groups are computed in that summand. Thus it is a weak homotopy equivalence, including when the index set is empty. The diagonal theorem gives $f\times1_K:X\times K\to X'\times K$ a weak homotopy equivalence. Factor $f\times g$ as $(1\times g)(f\times1)$ and use closure of weak equivalences under composition in the model structure of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. By induction this proves preservation of weak homotopy equivalences by finite products, including the empty product (the point). The same summand argument proves preservation by any coproduct indexed by a fixed small set.

source.place: Proof 10.6(ii): product and disjoint-union argument, with the diagonal theorem written explicitly.

proof.text: For either pair $(C,W)=(A,U)$ or $(B,V)$ put $E^w_{C,p}(a,b)=Z_w^{(C_p,W_p)}(a,b)$ using [def-coef-zigzag-homotopy-calculus]. Applying an operator of $C,W$ to arrows defines the simplicial diagram of categories $E^w_C(a,b)$. A $q$-simplex of its ordinary nerve is a string of $q$ commuting vertical diagrams, hence exactly the rectangular diagram defining $D^w_{C,W}(a,b)_{p,q}$. Composing the string is deletion of a row, and inserting an identity is repetition of a row. Thus $\mathsf N(E^w_C(a,b))=\operatorname{diag}D^w_{C,W}(a,b)$, naturally in $S$. For length zero $E$ is the terminal category if $a=b$ and the empty category otherwise; its map under $S$ is the identity. For $w=(+)$ every vertical arrow is an endpoint identity, so each $E_p$ is the discrete category on $C_p(a,b)$ and $\mathsf N(E)=C(a,b)$. For $w=(-)$ it is the discrete category on $W_p(b,a)$ and $\mathsf N(E)=W(b,a)$. The hypotheses on $S$ prove the conclusion for all words of length zero or one.

source.place: Definition 5.1 and Lemma 5.7: identify the nerve and start induction on word length.

proof.text: For nonempty words $u,v$ fix $x,y$ and, for a varying $z$, set $L_p(z)=E^u_{C,p}(x,z)$ and $R_p(z)=E^v_{C,p}(z,y)$. The action of $h:z\to z'$ in $W_p$ is composition at the free endpoint. $L$ is covariant when the last letter of $u$ is $+$ (postcompose its last arrow with $h$), and contravariant when it is $-$ (precompose its last arrow with $h$). $R$ is contravariant when the first letter of $v$ is $+$ (precompose its first arrow with $h$), and covariant when it is $-$ (postcompose its first arrow with $h$). Leave all other arrows fixed. Apply the same operation to the endpoint square of a morphism. Commutation of that square shows this is a functor; associativity and identities give strict functoriality in $h$. The simplicial operators preserve composition, so these endpoint functors are transfunctors on $W$ in the explicit sense of [lem-coef-two-sided-simplicial-grothendieck-invariance]. The maps induced by $S$ commute strictly with every endpoint action and simplicial operator.

source.place: Examples 9.3 and 10.3: endpoint actions and their simplicial compatibility; left-to-right word convention.

proof.text:
Let $*$ denote the constant transfunctor with value the terminal category. With the left-to-right word convention, the following degreewise two-sided Grothendieck constructions (as defined in [lem-coef-two-sided-simplicial-grothendieck-invariance]) are isomorphic to $E^{uv}_C(x,y)$:
$$\begin{array}{c|c}
(\operatorname{last}(u),\operatorname{first}(v))&E^{uv}_C(x,y)\\
(+,+)&R\otimes_W L\\
(-,-)&L\otimes_W R\\
(+,-)&*\otimes_W(L\times R)\\
(-,+)&(L\times R)\otimes_W *.
\end{array}$$
On objects concatenate the left and right diagrams at their common endpoint $z$. A morphism of the concatenated diagram consists of the vertical arrow $h:z\to z'$ at the cut and the two restrictions of its commuting squares. In the $(+,+)$ case those restrictions are $r\to R(h)r'$ and $L(h)l\to l'$; in the $(-,-)$ case they are $l\to L(h)l'$ and $R(h)r\to r'$; in the $(+,-)$ case they are $L(h)l\to l'$ and $R(h)r\to r'$; in the $(-,+)$ case they are $l\to L(h)l'$ and $r\to R(h)r'$. These are exactly the three-component morphisms of the respective construction. Conversely, glue those restrictions and the given $h$ to recover every square. These operations are inverse on objects and morphisms. Composition is vertical composition and gives the composition formula in the cited definition; the simplicial operators preserve the two restrictions and $h$. Hence these are isomorphisms of simplicial diagrams of categories, natural under $S$. No identity column is removed and no adjacent columns are composed.

source.place: Proposition 9.4 and Example 10.3: all four joins, with directions reversed from the printed word convention.

proof.text: Induct on $l\geq2$, assuming the asserted weak equivalence for every word of length less than $l$ and every pair of endpoints in $O$. Write $w=uv$ with $u$ of length $l-1$ and $v$ the last letter, so both words are nonempty. In Step 4 use $W=U$ for $C=A$ and $W=V$ for $C=B$. The base functor $H=S|_U:U\to V$ fixes the small object set $O$ and is a weak homotopy equivalence on every mapping set by the second hypothesis. Step 3 supplies strict transformations from the $A$-side endpoint transfunctors to pullbacks of the $B$-side endpoint transfunctors. At every $z$, the induction hypothesis for $(x,z)$ and $(z,y)$ gives weak equivalences on the diagonal nerves of $L$ and $R$. In the mixed-sign cases, the nerve and its diagonal commute with binary products because a composable string in a product category is a pair of strings; Step 1 therefore gives the required weak equivalence on the $L\times R$ fiber. The terminal transfunctor comparison is the identity. Thus every hypothesis of [lem-coef-two-sided-simplicial-grothendieck-invariance] holds in each of the four rows, and it gives a weak homotopy equivalence on the diagonal nerves of their total constructions. All fiber categories are small: their objects and morphisms are finite diagrams in the small categories $A_p,B_p$, and taking their families over small $O$ fits the fixed larger universe of that node.

source.place: Lemma 5.7, using Example 10.3 and Propositions 10.4–10.5: simultaneous induction for all endpoints.

proof.text: Under the isomorphisms in Step 4, the functor on total constructions in Step 5 sends each component arrow in both subdiagrams and the cut arrow $h$ to its image under $S$. It is therefore exactly the functor $E^w_A(x,y)\to E^w_B(x,y)$, not a chosen comparison with the same endpoints. Step 2 identifies its diagonal nerve with the specified map $\operatorname{diag}D^w_{A,U}(x,y)\to\operatorname{diag}D^w_{B,V}(x,y)$. This completes the induction, including the zero- and one-letter cases already checked. Identity columns and equal-direction neighbors were allowed throughout, as required.

source.place: Conclusion of Lemma 5.7: identify the induced map on unreduced fixed-word diagrams.

proof_origin.place: Explicit word-length induction and all four Grothendieck joins following Lemma 5.7, Proposition 9.4, Example 10.3 and Propositions 10.4–10.5, printed pp.24,31,33–34. Source read online; no local archival copy exists. Product step supplied using the existing diagonal theorem.
